title: Steve Eisman Shares the Real Story Behind Predicting the 2008 Crash | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 20
summary: Melissa Lee probes Eisman’s long-term technology optimism, trade uncertainty and historical subprime research. His strongest framework is loan-vintage analysis, attention to documentation and retained risk, and separating a compelling thesis from timing. He remains bullish on US technology and expects more M&A, while disclosing Apple, other large technology, PJT, Apollo and Moody’s positions. The current macro explanations are less tightly evidenced. Claims that officials knew nothing about AIG before Lehman and that Apple manufactures entirely in China are contradicted by primary records; reserve-currency status also does not imply unlimited fiscal freedom.
assessment: Full transcript read. This bounded evidence audit retains unresolved outcomes where matched primary verification is missing; those are not adverse accuracy grades.
speaker_map_notes: Melissa Lee interviews Steve Eisman. Lee’s questions and challenges are not counted as Eisman assertions; he explicitly adopts or rejects premises in his answers. Most substantive claims here are Eisman’s.
framework_points: Compare loan vintages at equal seasoning.
Wait for observable deterioration after forming a structural suspicion.
Study borrowing costs, execution and legal mechanics before changing instruments.
Distinguish aggregate growth from regional outcomes.
Assess bank capital separately from pre-crisis reputational narratives.
Keep conditional trade risks distinct from base-case forecasts.
tools_and_charts: Stock borrow fees and CDS contracts
Sector weights and adjusted technology classification
transcript_cautions: Opening montage repeats later interview content.
The early phrase captioned long time ago is clarified immediately by repeated long-term bullish language.
Recording references early-August jobs data and the already recorded venture interview; publication is August 11.

Tarullo’s title and dates are misremembered: official biography says Board service January 2009-April 2017 and supervision committee chair. This is a supporting chronology caution, not a principal investment verdict.
Household’s specific rate illustration and some old bankruptcy/position claims are retrospective and lack trade records.
Company-name caption errors include Providian, Comerica, Norfolk Southern and New Century.

claims.claim: Until a credible alternative to Treasuries exists, the United States can essentially do whatever it wants fiscally.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Establish whether the stated reserve unlimited fiscal proposition holds using matched primary disclosures; retain its conditions and separate causal explanations from price movements.
claims.reason: The conclusion does not follow from the premise. Assume Treasuries remain the leading reserve asset but investors require a higher yield as expected inflation or issuance rises. The reserve ranking can remain unchanged while debt-service costs rise and fiscal choices narrow. This is a valid counterexample to the asserted necessity of an alternative; it does not predict a crisis date.

claims.claim: Most venture capital outside AI and a few hot sectors remains in a prolonged depression that headline AI fundraising obscures.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Establish whether the stated vc bifurcation proposition holds using matched primary disclosures; retain its conditions and separate causal explanations from price movements.
claims.reason: NVCA’s later data confirm extraordinary AI concentration, difficult emerging-manager fundraising and limited distributions. Most and depression are not precisely defined, so the whole-sector claim is not fully resolved.

evidence.title: PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor, Q3 2026 overview
evidence.finding: AI represented 82.7% of year-to-date deal value. Funds of $500 million or more captured 78.1% of fundraising; fourth-or-later funds captured 88.2%. First-time managers had 4.5%, while exit constraints limited distributions. These statistics support concentration, not a precise forecast of surviving firms.

claims.claim: Apple manufactures all its products in China; production described as Indian manufacturing merely reassembles Chinese-made goods.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Establish whether the stated apple all china proposition holds using matched primary disclosures; retain its conditions and separate causal explanations from price movements.
claims.reason: Apple’s pre-episode 2024 filing expressly places manufacturing in multiple countries including India, Japan, Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam. Heavy Chinese dependence is distinct from 100% Chinese manufacturing, and the filing does not support the blanket reassembly claim.

evidence.title: Apple fiscal 2024 Form 10-K
evidence.finding: Apple disclosed manufacturing in whole or part in China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam before the episode. Trade restrictions and concentrated outsourcing are material risks. It does not say all components are manufactured in China or that Indian operations only reassemble completed Chinese products.

claims.next_check: No further outcome check is required for the bounded proposition; reassess only if source corrections or the stated assumptions change.

claims.claim: Apple’s manufacturing concentration makes it vulnerable to a US-China trade conflict despite his continued unhedged ownership.

claims.test: Establish whether the stated apple china risk proposition holds using matched primary disclosures; retain its conditions and separate causal explanations from price movements.
claims.reason: Apple itself identifies trade and concentrated outsourcing risks, supporting the vulnerability. The 100% China premise is wrong, and the claim that it has no possible adaptation is too strong. No trade-conflict earnings counterfactual or hedge return is established.
